question: A risk consultant is advising an Australian bank that currently validates all 240 of its AUD models with the same depth and on the same schedule. She recommends that the MRM function tier the models instead. Which of the following best describes the characteristics usually used to tier models and what the tier then determines?

options.B: Materiality of output, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use; the tier dictates the frequency of validation, while its thoroughness is the same for all models.

| M1 | No | Yes | 40.0 | High | 9 |
| M2 | No | No | 0.3 | Low | 2 |
| M3 | Yes | No | 6.0 | Medium | 1 |

Which proposed treatment is most consistent with good model risk management practice?

options.A: Rank the models by years in use and place M3 in the highest tier, since the newest model has the shortest performance record.

**Concept and theory**

Tiering ranks models by the risk they pose, using four characteristics: materiality of output (the size of the loss an error could cause), complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use. question: A risk consultant reviewing the MRM framework of a US bank is asked to describe how the performance of models is monitored between scheduled validations and reviews. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.A: Model owners produce monitoring reports, usually as per MRM standards, at intervals suited to how often each model is used, and MRM monitors performance through them.
options.B: MRM produces monitoring reports, as per its own standards, at intervals suited to how often each model is used, and model owners monitor performance through them.

Scheduled validations and annual reviews leave gaps in which a model can drift. GARP closes the gap with ongoing monitoring: “Beyond these regularly scheduled validations and reviews, MRM groups monitor the performance of models through the monitoring reports produced by model owners (usually as per MRM standards). question: A risk committee member at a Japanese bank notes that, although MRM is meant to be a continuous effort, the bank’s MRM function still works almost entirely through scheduled, point-in-time validations and reviews. Which of the following best explains why many institutions still operate in this way?

options.A: A periodic model is predictable, so staffing needs are predictable and much smaller validation teams can move from one scheduled task to the next.
options.B: A periodic model eliminates the risk that a model continues in use after it has stopped producing reliable forecasts between two validations.
options.C: A periodic model suits dynamic environments better, because models that need frequent recalibration are best reviewed at fixed dates.
options.D: A periodic model is unavoidable, because model owners are not expected to produce any monitoring reports between scheduled validations.

solution:
Risk committee member at a Japanese bank asking why MRM remains point in time rather than continuous.

**Concept and theory**

GARP sets a clear best practice: “Model risk management should be seen as a continuous effort rather than a point-in-time exercise revolving around validations and reviews.” It adds that this “is still one of the biggest challenges faced by many institutions.”

Why do institutions cling to the periodic model? GARP gives the operating reason: “Focusing on periodic rather than continuous validations is a more manageable operating model, a model that is predictable, which makes staffing needs predictable. It allows banks to operate much smaller teams of validators because once validators are done with a validation or review, they can move on to the next scheduled task […]

options.A: Acceptable: once MRM, as the independent second line, has validated a model, ownership of the model’s risk passes from the modelling team to MRM.

question: At a mature UK insurer, the modelling teams have formed their own quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) team. A newly appointed chief compliance officer asks how this team fits into model risk management. Which of the following best describes its role?

options.A: It is part of the second line, acting as MRM’s own quality team, and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.
options.B: It is the first line’s risk team and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly the risk of conceptual errors.
options.C: It is the first line’s risk team and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.
options.D: It is the first line’s risk team and, by mitigating execution risk, removes the need for independent validation by the second line.

solution:
Chief compliance officer at a mature UK insurer asks how the first-line QA/QC team fits into model risk management.

**Concept and theory**

The first line does not discharge its ownership of model risk only through individual developers’ diligence. GARP notes: “At more mature institutions, the modeling teams will form a quality control/quality assurance team. These QA/QC teams are the first line’s risk team and play a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.”

Why execution risk in particular? Execution risk arises when a model does not do what it is intended and designed to do, through coding errors, implementation errors, use of the wrong data and so on. question: A validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing an SGD mortgage prepayment model. She and the developer hold different views on a key prepayment assumption, and both views are reasonable and equally valid. The developer has noted the assumption’s limitations in the model documentation. Which course of action best reflects the role of MRM in this situation?

options.A: Decide which view of the assumption is correct and require the developer to adopt it, since conceptual questions of this kind are ultimately a matter of right or wrong.
options.B: Ensure transparency, making sure the assumption and its limitations are communicated to users so that they understand when the model can be safely used and when to stop.
options.C: Accept the assumption without further action, since limitations that are discussed in the model documentation can be relied on to be understood by all users.
options.D: Remove the conceptual risk entirely by requiring the developer to recalibrate the model until it is shown to be valid in every possible market environment.

solution:
Validator at a Singapore bank and a developer hold equally reasonable but different views on a prepayment assumption.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two sources of model risk. Execution errors are errors in doing what the model is designed to do; they are matters of right or wrong. Conceptual errors arise from wrong assumptions or techniques and are “much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong. Different reasonable modelers can have different and equally valid opinions on an assumption.”

The copula case is GARP’s illustration of a conceptual error: a model that is “right” in one context and “completely wrong” if the context changes. Nothing in the code needs to be broken for this to happen. The chain of cause and effect in the case runs as follows:

question: The head of model risk management at a Brazilian bank meets business heads who use a BRL credit portfolio pricing model. They say: “We cannot understand this model, and making sure that it works is the modellers’ job.” Which of the following responses is most consistent with the lesson of the Gaussian copula case?

options.A: Accept the position, because model performance is the modellers’ responsibility, and users without a quantitative background need not understand the model’s limitations.
options.B: Require every user to complete quantitative training to the modellers’ level before using the model, because only technically expert users can understand its limitations.

**Concept and theory**

The copula case ends with a lesson about people rather than mathematics. GARP says that “the most important skill required for the MRM function to be successful with this challenge is effective communication”. The reasoning is:

1. Most users of models at financial institutions do not have a quantitative background.
2. It is easy for them to “deflect responsibility by simply relying on the argument that they cannot understand the model and that it is the modelers’ responsibility to ensure that it works”.
3. A good MRM function “will help users understand in non-technical terms what the limitations are to minimize the mis-use of the models”.

loText: Explain the implications of further adoption of AI on financial stability.
question: An IMF economist explains why AI adoption raises monitoring and opacity challenges for the financial system. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Capital market and trading activity is shifting from banks, which face stringent transparency and model validation requirements, toward NBFIs under lighter oversight, while AI-generated portfolios create new correlations across regions, venues, and asset classes.
options.B: Banks face lighter model validation requirements than NBFIs, so the shift of activity toward banks reduces system-wide transparency.
options.C: Interconnectedness across markets declines as AI diversifies portfolios more effectively than human managers.
options.D: Opacity concerns are confined to the banking sector, where model complexity is greatest.

solution:
**Concept tested:** the opacity mechanism. Intuition: the activity is moving from the glass house (banks, heavy validation and disclosure) to the tinted-window house (NBFIs), while AI links markets in new ways that raise correlations and interconnectedness.

**Solution:** (a) is correct. Both halves are the stated mechanism: the bank-to-NBFI shift under asymmetric oversight, and new AI-generated cross-market linkages.

question: During model validation, a reviewer flags a GenAI output pattern: the model produces highly confident responses that are factually incorrect. Within the model risk terminology of the reading, this pattern is best described as:

options.A: Misalignment.
options.B: Hallucination.
options.C: Model poisoning.
options.D: Disinformation.

solution:
**Concept tested:** the hallucination definition among its siblings. Intuition: hallucination is the model's own confident error; poisoning is someone corrupting it; misalignment is it pursuing the wrong objective; disinformation is a malicious human broadcasting falsehoods.

**Solution:** (b) is correct. A hallucination is a highly confident but incorrect response, a GenAI-associated model inaccuracy.

loText: Explain the implications of further adoption of AI on financial stability.
question: The head of market risk at an Australian bank plans to use a pre-trained LLM, the same core model licensed by most of the bank’s peers, in two ways: (1) to build volatility and liquidity risk models that predict how heightened volatility would affect the trading book, to generate advanced stress scenarios, and to suggest hedges and risk limits; (2) to draft internal policy documents and retrieve information for staff training. An internal auditor reviewing the plan must state the financial-stability implication. Which of the following assessments is correct?

options.A: Use (2) carries higher market correlation risk than use (1), because back-oﬀice drafting and retrieval are the most widespread uses of LLMs across the industry.
options.B: Circuit breakers and transparency requirements fully eliminate the correlation vulnerability, so the bank need not monitor how the LLM’s risk outputs move with those of its peers.
options.C: Validation and outcome analysis of the LLM’s risk models should be governed by the vendor’s own model risk standards rather than by the bank’s existing model risk framework.
options.D: Use (1) raises market correlation risk relative to use (2), because models sharing architectures and training data produce correlated outputs that can amplify volatility and liquidity crunches in stress.

solution:
**Step 1 – Classify the two uses**

Use (1) is AI in market risk: the FSB lists volatility and liquidity risk management (models predicting how heightened volatility affects positions) among operations use cases, and the IMF lists advanced risk scenarios and dynamic risk sensing under risk management. Use (2) is back-oﬀice: information retrieval, employee training, document drafting.

**Step 2 – Apply the correlation channel**

Pre-trained core models share architectures and training data, so their outputs are naturally correlated. If LLMs inform risk management or investment strategy, correlation risk is higher; if they address internal back-oﬀice ineﬀiciencies, it is far lower.
